correctness.rationale: The boundary-one length-two symmetry follows directly from the published triangle relation: on three consecutive vertices all four boundary factors are \(1\), forcing \(c_{i,i+2}=c_{i+2,i}\). Applying the two oriented published exchange relations to four consecutive vertices of the pentagon gives \(q_i=q_{i+1}^{-1}+q_{i+1}^{-1}q_{i+3}\) and \(q_i=q_{i+1}^{-1}+q_{i+3}q_{i+1}^{-1}\); multiplying on the appropriate side yields \(q_iq_{i+1}=q_{i+1}q_i=1+q_{i+3}\). Thus adjacent quiddity entries commute. Since \(q_i\) also commutes with \(q_{i+4}\) and \(q_{i+4}=q_{i+1}q_{i+2}-1\), cancellation by the unit \(q_{i+1}\) gives \(q_iq_{i+2}=q_{i+2}q_i\). Every pair on five indices has cyclic distance one or two, so all pentagon values commute. The height-one relation \(ab=2\) makes its two internal units commute, while the cited quaternionic height-three example contains noncommuting quaternion units, proving sharpness of the height threshold.

value.rationale: The theorem identifies a sharp structural threshold: boundary-one noncommutativity is impossible for quadrilateral and pentagon friezes over any division ring, while a quaternionic height-three example exists. That is a natural complete low-height classification and explains where genuinely noncommutative behavior can first occur; it is more than a tiny numerical instance or arbitrary slice.
risks: The theorem does not classify all commuting pentagon friezes or arbitrary boundary coefficients.

limitations: Only boundary-one heights one and two are classified; arbitrary coefficients and higher-height classifications are outside scope.
